items.followUp: Differentiate between static friction and sliding friction.

rubric.why: Checks that sliding friction is linked to surfaces sliding relative to one another.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it acts when one surface slides over another.

rubric.why: The key comparison is that rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction.
rubric.description: Compares rolling friction with sliding friction.
rubric.how: Award for stating that rolling friction is less than sliding friction.

modelAnswer: Sliding friction acts when one surface slides over another and opposes their relative motion.
Rolling friction acts when an object rolls over a surface; it is less than sliding friction.

items.followUp: A cyclist increases speed from 2 m s⁻¹ to 14 m s⁻¹ in 4 s. Find the acceleration.

rubric.why: Checks use of the acceleration relation and the initial and final velocities.
rubric.description: States the formula and substitutes the velocity values and time.
rubric.how: Award for a correct formula with appropriate substitution.

rubric.why: Checks the calculated acceleration and its SI unit.

modelAnswer: Given: u = 0 m s⁻¹, v = 20 m s⁻¹, t = 8 s.
Formula: a = (v − u)/t.
Substitution: a = (20 m s⁻¹ − 0 m s⁻¹)/8 s.
Answer: a = 2.5 m s⁻².

items.followUp: Define torque and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Torque is the turning effect or moment of a force.
rubric.how: Award for identifying torque as the turning effect of a force.

rubric.why: The SI unit is the newton metre.
rubric.how: Award for the correct SI unit.

modelAnswer: Torque is the turning effect of a force about a pivot or axis.
Its SI unit is the newton metre (N m).

items.followUp: How do you find the resultant of two vectors using the head-to-tail rule?

rubric.why: Checks the placement of vectors in the head-to-tail arrangement.
rubric.description: Explains how the vectors are arranged.
rubric.how: Award for placing the tail of each following vector at the head of the preceding vector.

rubric.why: The resultant is the vector joining the start of the first vector to the end of the last.
rubric.how: Award for stating the correct direction and endpoints of the resultant.

modelAnswer: Place the tail of each vector at the head of the preceding vector, keeping their magnitudes and directions unchanged.
The resultant is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.

items.followUp: Define power and write its formula in terms of work and time.

rubric.why: Power is defined as the rate at which work is done.
rubric.how: Award for stating that power is work done per unit time.

rubric.why: Checks the standard formula for power.

modelAnswer: Power is the rate at which work is done.
Formula: P = W/t.

items.followUp: Define energy and give one example of an object possessing kinetic energy.

rubric.why: Energy is defined as the capacity to do work.
Checks for a valid example of an object or system with energy.
rubric.how: Award for one valid example, such as a moving car.

modelAnswer: Energy is the capacity to do work.
Example: a moving car possesses kinetic energy.

items.followUp: Define density and calculate it for a body of mass 6 kg and volume 2 m³.

rubric.why: Density is mass per unit volume.
Checks the formula relating density, mass, and volume.

modelAnswer: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance.
Formula: ρ = m/V.

items.followUp: State Hooke’s law and write the relation between force and extension.

rubric.why: Hooke’s law applies only within the elastic limit.
rubric.description: States the condition for Hooke’s law.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning the elastic limit.

rubric.why: The law states that extension is directly proportional to applied force within the elastic limit.
rubric.how: Award for the correct force-extension relationship.

modelAnswer: Within the elastic limit, the extension of an elastic object is directly proportional to the applied force.
In symbols, F ∝ x (or F = kx).
